description: Question: how contagious is seasonal influenza, and what does that number imply? An epidemic in a susceptible population first grows exponentially, I(t) ∝ e^(rt), and the growth rate r together with the generation interval gives the reproduction number R. Data: CDC's US outpatient surveillance week by week since the 2016–17 season (Delphi Epidata: FluView wILI and the clinical labs' percent positive), combined into ILI+, the standard proxy for influenza incidence. Steps: per season the peak, the growth window (5–60% of the peak, before it) and r as the slope of ln(ILI+); then R = (1 + r·Tg/k)^k (Wallinga & Lipsitch, generation interval 3 days, gamma k = 4) and the SIR model's consequences: the herd-immunity threshold 1 − 1/R, the final size z = 1 − e^(−Rz) and the peak prevalence. Aha: on a log axis every season's rise is a straight line, and a gentle one: ILI+ doubles in 8 to 20 days (median about 14), which means an effective R of only 1.1–1.3 in the eight seasons fitted. Influenza spreads barely above the epidemic threshold: immunising or preventing 10–20% of transmissions stops growth, where measles (R0 12–18) needs over 90%. Yet even so small an R would infect 18–40% of a fully susceptible SIR population, about twice the threshold, because the epidemic overshoots it. Caveats: ILI+ is a proxy, not a count; R depends on the assumed generation interval; it is the effective R at the season's start (prior immunity, vaccination), not R0; seasons with two waves fit less well (read fit_r2); 2020–21 and 2021–22 had too little influenza to fit; SIR ignores school terms, age structure and behaviour; eight seasons are few for the study. Next: hover a week or a season; drill down to HHS regions or states (same API, regions=hhs1…hhs10); expand to subtypes or vaccination coverage.
name: Influenza's R: exponential growth, herd immunity and final size
